newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang meets Vietnam's Do Muoi in Beijing.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang meets Vietnam's Do Muoi in Beijing.

text.p: Chinese Communist Party Secretary Jiang Zemin on Monday met his Vietnamese counterpart Do Muoi and said the two nations, at odds over waters in the South China Sea, should solve differences in a friendly manner.

Do Muoi arrived in Beijing on Monday for a five-day visit in the wake of a dispute over Chinese oil drilling in waters of the South China Sea that are claimed by both Beijing and Hanoi, and met Jiang just hours later, the Xinhua news agency said.

Fast development of friendly relations between China and Vietnam had formed a good basis for solving problems left over from history between the two nations, Xinhua quoted Jiang, who is also president and chief of China's military, as saying.

"If the two sides can stand tall, see far, take in the big picture, mutually understand and give in to each other... and if leaders of the two nations make great efforts to push forward, then problems can be quickly resolved in an appropriate manner," Xinhua quoted Jiang as telling Du Muoi.
Du Muoi echoed Jiang's words, saying Vietnam placed great importance on its relations with China.
"Vietnam hopes that leftover problems between the two nations can be solved more rapidly through peaceful consultations," Xinhua quoted the 80-year-old Communist Party chief as saying.

Xinhua did not say what problems existed, but in March China and Vietnam traded accusations over Beijing's decision to move its Kan Tan III oil rig into an area roughly between the coast of central Vietnam and China's southern Hainan island.
Although the Kan Tan III rig was later withdrawn, subsequent talks in Beijing aimed at preventing a recurrence failed to find common ground.
Do Muoi will meet other Chinese leaders on Tuesday, including Premier Li Peng, Qiao Shi, head of China's parliament, and Li Ruihuan, head of an advisory body to parliament, Chinese officials said.
China and Vietnam have a long history of animosity and distrust, despite their ideological similarities.
Chinese forces invaded in 1979 to punish Hanoi for its invasion of Cambodia. The brief but savage war that ensued cost at least 20,000 lives.
Tension over competing claims to sovereignty over the potentially oil-rich Paracel and Spratly islands has bubbled beneath the surface despite normalisation of relations in 1991.
In 1994, the two sides agreed to set up a group of experts to discuss their problems in the South China Sea.

Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and China's rival, Taiwan, have also staked claims to all or part of the scattered and barren Spratlys that straddle strategic sea lanes. China has occupied the Paracels since 1974.
An exchange of visits between Chinese and Vietnamese leaders in recent years has led to warmer bilateral relations.
Premier Li visited Vietnam in July last year after Do Muoi visited China in November 1995.
Vietnam refused to mourn the death in February of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, the man seen as being responsible for the 1979 Sino-Vietnamese border war.
